seoTitle: Michigan Labor & Delivery Negligence Lawyer – Injuries to Mother or Baby
seoDescription: Labor and delivery negligence in Michigan: Pitocin, delayed C-section, VBAC rupture, cord prolapse, forceps and vacuum, hemorrhage, preeclampsia, infection. The standard for each, the records that show it, both parents’ deadlines, and the 2026 caps. Free review.
h1: Labor and Delivery Negligence Lawyer Michigan
tagline: Two patients, one room, and a standard of care for every hour of it.
primaryKeyword: labor and delivery negligence lawyer michigan

c.v: Labor and delivery is the only hospital admission with two patients. Michigan hospitals delivered 99,420 babies in 2024; nearly a third were born by cesarean, and about one in fifty by vacuum or forceps. The overwhelming majority of those deliveries ended with a healthy mother and a healthy child. The ones that did not are the subject of this page: the labors in which a known complication was missed or mismanaged, and either the mother or the baby, or both, left the hospital with an injury that the standard of care existed to prevent.

Most pages on this subject are about the baby. That is understandable, because a child’s brain injury is the largest of these cases. But labor and delivery negligence injures mothers too, and Michigan’s own maternal mortality review found that three of every four pregnancy-related deaths in the state were preventable. Hemorrhage that was not measured until the mother was in shock, blood pressure that was not treated until she seized, a uterine rupture during an attempted vaginal birth after cesarean with no operating room ready, a fourth-degree tear that was never repaired: these are the mother’s own claims, with their own deadline, and they are brought alongside the child’s.

This page covers the complications of labor and delivery that most often become Michigan malpractice cases, the professional standard that applied to each, the records that show whether it was met, injuries to the baby and to the mother, who is liable, the damages and 2026 caps, and the deadlines, which differ for the mother and the child.

ATLAW is a personal injury firm in Dearborn. In 13 years the firm has handled more than 10,000 cases and recovered more than $100 million for clients across Wayne, Oakland, Macomb, and Washtenaw counties. Birth injury and maternal injury cases are handled on contingency: no fee unless we recover money for your family, and the first conversation is free.

c.v: One point of Michigan law matters particularly to injured mothers. The higher non-economic cap, $1,065,000 for 2026, applies not only to brain and spinal cord paralysis and permanent cognitive impairment but also to an injury to the reproductive system that leaves the patient unable to have children. A mother who lost her uterus because of negligent management of hemorrhage or uterine rupture may qualify for the higher cap when the injury resulted in an inability to procreate under MCL 600.1483(1)(c).

Michigan retains joint and several liability in medical malpractice where the plaintiff was without fault, MCL 600.6304(6).

Michigan requires proof of the standard of care, breach, causation more probable than not, and damages, MCL 600.2912a, through experts who practice the same specialty as the defendant, MCL 600.2169. A labor and delivery case typically needs a board-certified obstetrician, a labor and delivery nurse, and, depending on the injury, a maternal-fetal medicine specialist, an anesthesiologist, a neonatologist and pediatric neurologist for the child, a urogynecologist or colorectal surgeon for maternal pelvic injury, and life care and economic experts.

faqs.question: The baby is fine but I was badly injured. Do I have a case?

answer.v: Possibly. A mother’s injuries from mismanaged hemorrhage, untreated blood pressure, an unrepaired tear, a surgical injury during cesarean, or an anesthesia complication are malpractice claims in their own right. The deadline is two years from the malpractice, so do not wait.

faqs.question: I had a C-section after hours of labor. Was it too late?

answer.v: Not necessarily; many cesareans after a long labor are timely and appropriate. The question is what the fetal monitor showed and when, and how long the hospital took to deliver once the decision was made. The strip and the operating room log answer it.

faqs.question: I was told I could try a VBAC. The uterus ruptured. Is the hospital responsible?

answer.v: It depends on whether the risks were explained, whether you were an appropriate candidate, whether the signs of rupture were recognized promptly, and whether the hospital had the staff immediately available to perform an emergency cesarean, which is what the professional standard requires for any hospital offering a trial of labor after cesarean.

faqs.question: They used a vacuum three or four times and then forceps. Is that negligence?

answer.v: The professional guidance limits the number of pulls and detachments and discourages switching between instruments; a prolonged operative delivery that should have become a cesarean is a common claim. The newborn’s injuries, cephalohematoma or subgaleal hemorrhage in particular, and the operative note decide the case.

faqs.question: My blood pressure was high for hours before anyone treated it. Does that matter?

answer.v: Yes. A confirmed pressure of 160/110 or higher is a hypertensive emergency that the standard of care treats within 30 to 60 minutes. Delay risks eclampsia and stroke. The vital-sign flowsheet shows every reading and the medication record shows when treatment began.

faqs.question: I lost my uterus to bleeding after delivery. What is my claim worth?

answer.v: That depends on whether the hemorrhage was measured and treated according to the hospital’s own protocol and how quickly. If negligent care caused your injury, your economic damages are uncapped, and the permanent loss of a reproductive organ resulting in an inability to procreate may qualify for Michigan's higher non-economic cap, $1,065,000 for 2026.

The child: until the tenth birthday for an injury before age eight. The mother and father: two years. A death: two years with a saving provision. A university hospital: six months’ notice. The 182-day notice of intent precedes every suit.

faqs.question: Is the midwife liable, or the hospital?

answer.v: Potentially both. A certified nurse-midwife is held to the standard of care of her profession; the hospital is liable for its employees and for the physician backup and operating room access the midwifery service depends on.

faqs.question: Will we have to go to trial?

answer.v: Most Michigan labor and delivery cases resolve before trial after the experts have reviewed the records on both sides. We prepare every case to be tried.
